per_ply.human_comment:
Bogoljubov was considered a very good expert of
the Slave Defense. He had proved that the year before (1929) during his match
against Alekhine. But Mikenas did not care about that. He had studied openings
very carefully, and the strategic ideas and right in the Slave he had a
novelty. Was not this a good opportunity to test it?

In the first
game of his match against Alekhine Bogo tried to have an edge with 5... e6 6.
e4 Bb4 7. e5 Nd5 8. Bd2 Bxc3 9. bxc3 b5 but the World Champion reacted very
actively: 10.Ng5 f6 11. exf6 Nxf6 12. Be2 obtaining a position with many
possibilities of attack.

per_ply.system_comment: This is the last book move of the Slav Defense: Czech Variation, Wiesbaden Variation (D17); both sides are on their own from here.

The most accurate move, holding the balance (-0.03, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Bb4 e3 O-O Bxc4 c5], immediately targets the knight on c3—pressure that often forces awkward replies from White. In return, the continuation may leave Black's back rank vulnerable. Be7 is a comparable option that leads to equality via [pv:Be7 f3 h6 Bh4 c5], but Bb4 is preferred for its direct challenge to that knight.

The most accurate move, holding the balance (-0.03, Stockfish:16) along [pv:dxc5 Qa5 Qd4 Nc6 Nxc6], in return leaves Black's pawn structure improved—a lasting structural gain—as doubled, isolated, and backward pawn issues are eased. 9.e3 is a comparable option that leads to a slight advantage for Black with [pv:e3 h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 Bxc4], where the line may leave White with a knight for a bishop and could improve White's pawn structure. Later play may turn toward targeting the bishop on f5.

per_ply.system_comment: The most accurate move, holding the balance (-0.03, Stockfish:16) with [pv:Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6 e4 Bg6], as the continuation may leave Black's king safe—a secure king is much harder to attack. Bxc5 was a comparable option that leads to equality [pv:Bxc5 Qxc4 Nc6 Nxc6 bxc6], where Black immediately wins a pawn, yet Nc6 is stronger for the safer king prospects it sets up in the main line.

12.e4 is the strongest choice, holding the balance (+0.00, Stockfish:16) by immediately targeting the bishop on f5, with [pv:e4 Bg6 Be3 Rd8 Qxc4] set to win a pawn—a material edge that often tells in simplified endings. O-O-O was a comparable option, though it leads to a slight advantage for Black [pv:O-O-O Bxc5 Qxc4 O-O e4], activating the rooks on the open files and potentially improving piece activity, yet e4 keeps the position level while maintaining that pressure on f5.

The strongest continuation, holding the balance (+0.11, Stockfish:16) and steering play toward [pv:Bg6 Qa6 Qb6 Qxb6 axb6], where Black may open the a-file for the rook—open files give rooks active targets. At the cost of White's king becoming safer deeper in the line. Bxe4 is a comparable option that leads to a slight advantage for White [pv:Bxe4 fxe4 O-O Bxf6 gxf6], immediately weakening White's pawn structure while potentially stripping White of the bishop-pair edge later; Bg6 keeps the position more even.

per_ply.human_comment: Now, if 14.0-0 15.Nd1! Qb6 16.a5 White wins a piece. Black has no choice.

per_ply.system_comment: Where 14...Nd7 leads to equality and may open the h-file for Black's rook while leaving White's back rank vulnerable in the continuation, 14...Qb6 concedes a slight advantage to White (-0.16 → +0.44, Stockfish:16) [pv:Qb6 a5 Bf2+ Ke2 Qc5], as the queen sortie could leave White's king under pressure only after a5 and Bf2+. White's reply a5 keeps the initiative. 14...Nd7 leads to equality [pv:Nd7 h4 h5 Ne2 Qb6] as a comparable option.

The most accurate move, a5 maintains White's advantage. The pawn advance may leave Black with a hanging piece, push his pieces passive, and open the a-file for White's rook, though at the cost of White's own pieces potentially becoming passive in the continuation. (+0.43, Stockfish:16) [pv:a5 Bf2+ Ke2 Qc5 Qxc5] Nd1 leads to equality [pv:Nd1 a5 Rc1 Nd7 Qc3] and was a comparable option that could have activated White's rooks on the open files while weakening Black's pawn structure, but a5 preserves more of the edge.

Black's most accurate move, 16...Qc5, immediately targets the queen on c4, keeping White's queen under direct pressure. Still, it leads to a slight advantage for White (+0.44, Stockfish:16) [pv:Qc5 Qxc5 Bxc5 Na4 Bd4]. By comparison, 16...Qd8 gives White a winning advantage [pv:Qd8 Qxc6+ Kf8 Bf4 Bd4] even though it improves the pawn structure right away and may set up targeting of the knight on c3 deeper in the line, which is why Qc5 is clearly the stronger choice for Black.

The best move is Qxc5, which maintains White's advantage (+0.44, Stockfish:16) [pv:Qxc5 Bxc5 Na4 Bd4 Be3] by making the king safe and easing the pressure Black had been directing toward it—worth prioritizing when you already hold a small edge. Ra4 is a roughly comparable option that leads to equality [pv:Ra4 O-O Qxc5 Bxc5 Rc4], though that line could leave Black's back rank vulnerable after further exchanges.

Black's king is now safe after 17...Bxc5, the immediate gain from capturing on c5, though the move still leads to a slight advantage for White (+0.44, Stockfish:16) [pv:Bxc5 Na4 Bd4 Be3 c5]. When the king has been under pressure, securing it comes first. The capture is clearly stronger than 17...Bh4, which would leave White with a decisive advantage [pv:Bh4 g3 Bxg3 hxg3 Rc8]. Later,...Nd5 will target the bishop on e3, a piece that often anchors White's central coordination. The queens are off — the game enters its final phase, where technique matters more than tactics. The position stays balanced.

per_ply.human_comment:

per_ply.system_comment: Black passed up Nxe3, which leads to equality on [pv:Nxe3 Kxe3 Rhc8 Be2 e5], and played 26...c5 instead, conceding a slight advantage to White (+0.07 → +0.65, Stockfish:16) on [pv:c5 Bxc5 Bxc5+ Rxc5 Rac8]. The pawn push establishes a passed pawn on c5—a lever that can cramp the enemy in the endgame—and could open the c-file for Black's rook if play continues along that line, though White is set to contest the break at once. Nxe3, which leads to equality on [pv:Nxe3 Kxe3 Rhc8 Be2 e5], was the stronger try.

The most accurate move maintains White's advantage (+0.59, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Bxc5 Bxc5+ Rxc5 Rhc8 Rc4], immediately targeting the bishop on e7, at the cost of Black's rooks possibly becoming more active on the open files as the line continues. Be2 leads to equality on [pv:Be2 Nxe3 Kxe3 Rhd8 h4], a comparable option that actively places the pieces and could leave White with a knight for a bishop.

The most accurate move is 28...Rhc8, Black's best try even though it leads to a slight advantage for White (+0.69, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rhc8 Bd4 Bc2 b6 Nxb6], as it may set the king on a safer footing in the continuation. A comparable option is 28...Rhb8, which leads to a clear advantage for White on [pv:Rhb8 Nc3 Bf6 Nxd5 exd5], where White immediately leaves a piece hanging while White's pieces could grow more passive further down the line—a sharper route, but one that concedes more than the accurate rook lift.

per_ply.system_comment: Black's most accurate reply is 30...gxf6, which immediately strips White of the bishop-pair advantage—a pairing that often dominates open positions—though it still leaves White with a clear advantage (+0.85, Stockfish:16) on [pv:gxf6 Be2 Rxc4 Bxc4 Rc8] at the cost of conceding a pawn. Nxf6 is a comparable alternative that also leads to a clear advantage for White on [pv:Nxf6 Nb4 Rxc4 Bxc4 Kd6] and would have given Black immediate control of the center, but gxf6 is the stronger choice for eliminating White's two bishops.

Black missed the potential to leave White with a hanging piece—a target worth exploiting—by playing 31...Nb6 instead of 31...Bg6, which leads to a clear advantage for White on [pv:Bg6 Rd1 Ke7 Rdd4 Nb6]. That inaccuracy makes matters worse: White now has a winning advantage, and the evaluation jumps (+0.85 → +1.83, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nb6 Rd1+ Ke8 Rxc8+ Rxc8]. 31...Bg6 was the better retreat, still handing White a clear edge on [pv:Bg6 Rd1 Ke7 Rdd4 Nb6].

Rd1+ is the most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+1.84, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rd1+ Ke8 Rxc8+ Rxc8 Nb4], and immediately activates White's rooks on the open files — rooks on open lines are among the most effective pieces in the middlegame. In return, Black's king is now safer. Rxc8 is a roughly comparable option that leads to a clear advantage for White on [pv:Rxc8 Nxc8 Rd1+ Kc7 Rc1+], but Rd1+ is the stronger choice.

Black missed the chance to retreat with...Ke8, keeping the king safe and out of White's king-side pressure, and missed the potential to leave White's pieces passive once the rook trade on c8 unfolds. The engine had preferred Ke8 here; instead Ke7 makes matters worse, and White now has a winning advantage (+1.84 → +2.48, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Ke7 Rxc8 Rxc8 Nb4 Bc2]. Ke8 was the better try, though it still gives White a winning advantage, on [pv:Ke8 Rxc8+ Rxc8 Nb4 Rd8].

The most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+2.45, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rxc8 Rxc8 Nb4 Bc2 Rd2], immediately leaves Black's pieces passive and blunts their counterplay—often the practical way to press a winning edge—at the cost of White's own pieces growing slightly less active in return. Rh4 also leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:Rh4 Nd5 Nb4 Nxb4 Rxb4], but recapturing on c8 is the stronger continuation.

Recapturing on c8 with the rook fights back, though White still keeps a winning advantage (+2.09, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Rxc8 Nb4 Bc2 Rd2 Ba4]. Taking with the knight instead would have made the king safer but leaves White with a decisive advantage on [pv:Nxc8 Nb4 Nb6 g4 Bg6], so the rook recapture is the stronger try in a difficult endgame. White's accurate Nb4 next maintains the pressure along the same line. With so few pieces left, this is an endgame now: king activity and pawns decide it. White remains firmly better going into it.

White secures a strong knight on c6—a central outpost that restricts Black—and the line may build pressure against the knight on b6. g4 was a comparable option that gives White a winning advantage on [pv:g4 Bg6 Nc6+ Rxc6 bxc6], immediately targeting the bishop on f5 and setting up the potential to win the exchange further on.

By comparison, 36...Bc2 was a comparable option that also leaves White with a decisive advantage on [pv:Bc2 Rc1 Rxc6 bxc6 Ba4], immediately targeting the rook on d1 while the king may be safer deeper in that line—but Bg6 remains the stronger choice in a difficult endgame where White’s edge tends to grow in the moves ahead.

Rb8 is the most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+3.39, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rb8 Nd7 Rb7 Rxb7 axb7], in return for a line where Black's king may become safer and White's pieces could grow more passive. Nxa7 is a comparable option that gives White a winning advantage [pv:Nxa7 Rxa7 Rd6 Na8 b6], immediately obtaining a passed pawn on b5 and improving the pawn structure, yet Rb8 remains the strongest continuation.

40...Bd5 makes matters worse, and White now has a decisive advantage (+4.07 → +5.36, Stockfish:16). White is two pawns up—a margin that is tough to overturn in an endgame—and [pv:Bd5 Rxb6 Rxa7 Rb8 Rc7] shows the advantage growing. Black missed the chance to play Rxb7, which also leaves White with a decisive advantage [pv:Rxb7 axb7 Nd7 Nc6 h6].

Black's most accurate move is 41...Rxa7, the best try in a difficult endgame even though White retains a decisive advantage (+5.19, Stockfish:16), with the main line [pv:Rxa7 Rb8 Rd7 b6 Kg6]. The runner-up 41...Ba8 is clearly inferior—it too leaves White decisively ahead, but after [pv:Ba8 Rb8 Rxa7 b6 Rxa6] it puts up less stubborn resistance than the rook capture, and White went on to win.
